tldr: By using MPBRS, which shapes rewards via differences in potential functions, the authors achieved stable locomotion learning across nine distinct humanoid robots using a unified reward configuration without re-tuning any reward weights.
hero_caption: Comparison of walking postures learned with the Baseline (left), Direct Reward Shaping (DRS, middle), and the proposed MPBRS (right). While the baseline robot leans backwards, MPBRS acquires a natural, upright posture on par with carefully hand-tuned DRS.
overview:
Designing reward functions and tuning their weights is the biggest bottleneck in acquiring humanoid locomotion policies with reinforcement learning. Even a tiny imbalance in weights can cause robots to freeze in place or adopt bizarre postures—an issue known as reward hacking. To make matters worse, a reward setup that works on one robot rarely transfers to another with different leg lengths or joint kinematics, forcing practitioners into tedious trial-and-error tuning for every single platform.

To tackle this, the authors turned to Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS), which carries theoretical guarantees of preserving the optimal policy. Unlike conventional Direct Reward Shaping (DRS), which rewards desirable states directly, PBRS grants rewards only for the differences that represent progress toward a better state. This paper establishes a Multi-PBRS (MPBRS) framework incorporating three key terms—base height, uprightness, and joint symmetry—unifying the reward structure and weights across robots with only basic metadata such as joint names and default target heights.

Using the IsaacLab simulator, the authors evaluated this unified reward formulation across nine morphologically distinct humanoid robots (including Unitree G1/H1, Fourier N1, and others). They also carried out a sensitivity analysis, varying reward weights across a wide range from 0.1 to 500.

The results show that MPBRS achieves stable locomotion across all nine robots without re-tuning weights. While DRS causes the robots to freeze and abandon walking when weights are scaled up, MPBRS preserves the optimal policy and tracks target velocities even when weights are increased 500-fold. This practical study demonstrates that the true power of PBRS lies not merely in accelerating training, but in its exceptional insensitivity to weight tuning and its superior transferability across robots.
contributions: Extended Potential-Based Reward Shaping to formulate a unified Multi-PBRS (MPBRS) framework that simultaneously guides base height, uprightness, and joint symmetry.
Successfully trained locomotion policies across nine distinct humanoid robots using the exact same reward structure and weights without robot-specific re-tuning.

Empirically demonstrated through sensitivity analyses (varying weights from 0.1 to 500) that MPBRS avoids the freezing behavior seen in Direct Reward Shaping (DRS) and exhibits remarkable robustness to weight tuning.

sections.heading: Why does humanoid reinforcement learning fall into the "reward trap"?
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning is effective for full-body humanoid locomotion, reward weight tuning is notoriously delicate and difficult to transfer across robots. This paper leverages PBRS, which preserves optimal policies, to build a unified reward setup reusable across nine different robots.
sections.details:
In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved impressive results in humanoid robot locomotion control. It allows robots to autonomously discover full-body coordination that is otherwise difficult to design by hand. However, beneath this success lies a persistent issue: the quagmire of reward engineering.

For example, using simple squared-error penalties for velocity tracking often leads to unintended, unnatural movements—known as "reward hacking"—where the robot exploits bizarre postures just to accumulate reward. On the other hand, adding auxiliary shaping terms to encourage upright posture or smoothness creates an extremely delicate balance among reward weights. A slight tweak can cause the robot's gait to collapse or make it freeze entirely without taking a step.

Furthermore, humanoids have high degrees of freedom and complex contact dynamics with the ground. As a result, a reward setup laboriously tuned for one platform fails completely on another with different link lengths or actuator characteristics. Practitioners end up re-tuning weights from scratch for each robot, severely hurting reproducibility and transferability.

This is where Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS), introduced by Ng et al., becomes theoretically compelling. PBRS shapes rewards via the temporal difference (discounted difference) of a potential function, providing an elegant mathematical guarantee that it does not alter the optimal policy in a Markov Decision Process (MDP). While historically used to accelerate convergence in simple, low-dimensional toy tasks, this study reframes PBRS as a practical tool for tuning insensitivity and cross-morphology transferability. The authors propose a unified pipeline applied directly across nine morphologically diverse humanoids without redesigning the reward setup.

captions.F1: Comparison of walking postures learned under three settings. The Baseline (left) leans backwards in an unnatural posture, whereas MPBRS (right) achieves a stable, upright gait comparable to Direct Reward Shaping (DRS, center) with finely hand-tuned weights.

sections.heading: The limits of manual tuning and the re-evaluation of theoretical shaping
sections.summary: Direct auxiliary rewards (DRS) and imitation learning involve high tuning overhead and lack cross-robot transferability. Meanwhile, PBRS, previously used mostly for training acceleration in low-dimensional domains, is repositioned as a means to achieve robustness and portability in high-dimensional robotics.
sections.details:
### II-A Current State of Reward Shaping for Locomotion
Currently, the predominant approach in legged robot RL is Direct Reward Shaping (DRS). This method sums the absolute values of various terms at each step—such as maintaining an upright torso, holding pelvis height, and penalizing joint torques or accelerations alongside velocity tracking. While easy to compute, the magnitude of each term depends heavily on the robot's mass and sensor setup. Consequently, minor weight discrepancies lead to overly hesitant gaits or divergence.

Another prominent approach is imitation learning, which tracks reference motions such as motion capture data. While this produces natural motions quickly, collecting reference trajectories is labor-intensive, and the policies become overly anchored to the reference motions, making direct transfer to robots with different kinematic structures difficult.

### II-B The True Value of Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS)
Introduced by Ng et al. in 1999, PBRS adds the difference of a potential function representing "state goodness" to the reward, guiding exploration without disrupting the optimal policy. Past research has mostly discussed it in the context of how much it accelerates convergence in simple environments like grid worlds.

However, recent humanoid studies (such as work by Jeon et al.) report that in high-dimensional real-world tasks, PBRS provides only modest convergence speedups, but proves remarkably robust against reward scaling and weight changes. Capitalizing on this practical advantage, this study formulates Multi-PBRS combining multiple potential functions to run nine humanoids without re-tuning, opening up a new avenue of practical utility.

sections.heading: The mathematics of Multi-PBRS: Why difference-based rewards do not break
sections.summary: Unlike DRS, which rewards being in a good state, PBRS rewards only the transition (progress) toward a better state. This work formulates MPBRS by combining three potentials: base height, uprightness, and joint symmetry.
sections.details:
### III-A Markov Decision Processes and Problem Formulation
The robot locomotion task is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by a state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, transition probability distribution $\mathcal{T}$, base reward function $r$, and discount factor $\gamma \in (0, 1]$. The objective of reinforcement learning is to discover an optimal policy $\pi^*$ that maximizes the expected discounted return.

### III-B Key Difference: DRS vs. Multi-PBRS
When adding dense auxiliary rewards, intuitive DRS multiplies each desired state metric $\Phi_i(s_t)$ by a weight $w_i$ and directly adds them at each step:
$\hat{r}(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) = r(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) + \sum_i w_i \Phi_i(s_{t+1})$
Under this formulation, however, the robot receives continuous rewards simply by remaining in a desirable state. As a result, posture maintenance rewards easily overshadow the primary objective (moving forward), leading the robot to abandon walking and freeze upright.

In contrast, PBRS supplies auxiliary rewards as differences in potential functions:
$F(s_t, s_{t+1}) = \sum_i \omega_i \left( \gamma_\Phi \Phi_i(s_{t+1}) - \Phi_i(s_t) \right)$
Crucially, if the state remains unchanged, the contribution to the reward drops to near zero; positive reward is delivered only at the moment the robot improves toward a better state. This effectively prevents the policy from hacking the reward by standing still.

### Three Potential Designs in Multi-PBRS
This study adopts three shared potential terms across all robots:
- Base height potential $\phi_h(s)$: Increases as the pelvis height from the ground (determined via ray-casting) approaches the target value (Gaussian width $\sigma_h = 0.08$).
- Upright potential $\phi_{\text{up}}(s)$: Evaluates how vertically aligned the torso is using the z-component of the gravity vector in the base frame.
- Joint regularization potential $\phi_j(s)$: References a joint mapping dictionary to penalize deviations in ankle lateral symmetry and pelvis yaw from nominal poses (Gaussian width $\sigma_q = 0.5$).

Each potential is cached online, and on episode resets, rewards are initialized to zero to prevent anomalous boundary impulses. Following findings from prior literature, the discount factor is set to an undiscounted $\gamma_\Phi = 1.00$.

sections.heading: Training nine diverse humanoids simultaneously within a unified framework
sections.summary: Nine humanoid robots, including Fourier N1 and Unitree G1, were simulated in IsaacLab. Apart from a joint mapping dictionary and nominal base height, observations, base rewards, and PPO hyperparameters were kept entirely identical.
sections.details:
### IV-A The Nine Humanoid Platforms
The experiments evaluate nine humanoids spanning diverse sizes, masses, and joint kinematics: Fourier N1, Tienkung2, Unitree G1, Unitree H1, Booster T1, Fourier GR3V2, Kuavo S45, Hightorque HI, and Berkeley Humanoid Lite. For walking and running tasks, the arms are locked at nominal angles, controlling only the legs and pelvis yaw joints.

### IV-B Low-Level PD Control
The policy network outputs normalized target joint positions, which are converted into torques via per-joint PD controllers. To avoid torque saturation and ensure smooth motion, gains are tailored to each robot's actuator specifications per joint.

### IV-C Observation Space and Reward Configuration
The observation dimension is $18 + 3N_a$ (where $N_a$ is the number of actuated joints), restricted strictly to onboard IMU and encoder data without external camera tracking (base angular velocity, gravity vector, velocity commands, joint positions/velocities, and previous action). Uniform noise is injected to anticipate real-world transfer.
The base reward includes only two primary task terms: linear velocity tracking (forward and lateral) and yaw rate tracking; the remainder consists of regularization penalties on torques and action rate-of-change. Identical posture metrics are then added to compare DRS and MPBRS directly.

### IV-D Implementation and Training Environment
The setup uses NVIDIA IsaacLab as the simulator and PPO-Clip (from the RSL-RL library) as the algorithm. With a 200 Hz simulation frequency and 100 Hz control frequency, 2,048 parallel environments were trained on an accessible desktop featuring an Intel i7-9700F and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 (6 GB). Training 1,000 steps completes in approximately 50 minutes.

captions.F2: The nine humanoid robots lined up in IsaacLab. From right to left: Fourier N1, Tienkung2, Unitree G1, Unitree H1, Booster T1, Fourier GR3V2, Kuavo S45, Hightorque HI, and Berkeley Humanoid Lite, highlighting differences in size and kinematic structures.

sections.heading: Rock solid even at 500x weight! Astonishing tuning tolerance and generality
sections.summary: Training converged reliably across all nine robots under identical weights. Sensitivity analyses further revealed that while DRS induces freezing as weights grow, MPBRS maintains velocity tracking performance even with weights scaled up to 500.
sections.details:
### V-A Benchmark Comparison Across Nine Robots
Policies converged across all nine platforms under all three conditions: Baseline, DRS, and MPBRS.
Looking at total reward curves, DRS appears to rise faster initially, but this is merely an artifact of adding raw auxiliary values that inflate the overall reward scale. The critical metric is task completion: evaluating linear velocity ($x$-$y$) and yaw rate ($z$) tracking shows that all three methods eventually reach similarly high tracking accuracy.
Remarkably, even though the MPBRS weight was fixed at 1.0 across every robot, fall rates decreased steadily and natural gaits were acquired across all nine robots. Convergence speed was also observed to depend on each robot's inertia and joint limits.
Furthermore, velocity tracking tests on Fourier N1 demonstrated high robustness: even when forcibly respawned every 10 seconds, tracking errors dropped rapidly right after, smoothly following high-speed forward walking commands up to 3.5 m/s.

### V-B Sensitivity Analysis on Reward Weights (Unmatched Robustness)
To thoroughly evaluate robustness, the authors conducted a sensitivity analysis varying auxiliary reward weights from 0.1 to 500.
In DRS, as weights increased, height and uprightness terms became overly dominant, causing the robot to ignore velocity commands entirely and collapse into a stationary standing solution. At a weight of 500, tracking error failed to decrease at all.
In contrast, under MPBRS, the robot continued to track commanded velocities accurately even at an extreme weight of 500. Because shaping rewards converge to zero as the potential approaches the target state, the auxiliary term does not distort the policy gradients of the primary velocity tracking task regardless of how massive its weight is. This clearly proves that practitioners no longer need to worry about fine-tuning reward weights in practice.

captions.F3: Learning curve comparisons across the nine humanoids for Baseline, DRS, and MPBRS. From top to bottom: total reward, fall rate, XY velocity tracking reward, and yaw velocity tracking reward. While DRS shows inflated total rewards due to additive auxiliary terms, MPBRS converges stably to comparable or superior velocity tracking accuracy.
captions.F4: Velocity tracking performance of the MPBRS policy on Fourier N1. Despite forced respawns (resets) at 10-second intervals, the policy quickly recovers from error spikes and accurately tracks forward velocity commands up to 3.5 m/s.
captions.F5: Sensitivity analysis when varying shaping weights from 0.1 to 500. In DRS (top), velocity tracking reward drops sharply as weights increase, whereas in MPBRS (bottom), high tracking rewards are consistently maintained even at an extreme weight of 500.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook: Toward a unified foundation for humanoid RL
sections.summary: MPBRS provides extreme insensitivity to weight tuning and seamless cross-robot transferability rather than dramatic training speedups. Future directions include adaptive potentials and real-world deployment (Sim-to-Real).
sections.details:
This work proposed and validated Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping (MPBRS), applying a single unified reward configuration across nine distinct humanoid robots.

The key takeaway is that for high-dimensional humanoid locomotion, the true value of PBRS lies not in faster convergence, but in its exceptional robustness to weight scaling and seamless cross-platform transferability. Because it avoids warping the underlying objective function unlike direct shaping, it encourages upright posture and height retention early on while naturally guiding exploration toward the true task-optimal policy. This liberates roboticists from the grueling cycle of tuning reward weights dozens of times for each new robot.

For future work, the authors highlight integrating neural networks to learn and adapt potential functions, modeling advanced sensor noise for sim-to-real transfer, and combining domain randomization. As a unified pipeline that dramatically streamlines reinforcement learning for bipedal locomotion, MPBRS represents an exciting foundation for future developments.

takeaways: The true benefit of PBRS lies not in faster training, but in its exceptional insensitivity to reward weight tuning and seamless transferability across robot morphologies.

Direct Reward Shaping (DRS) collapses into local minima such as freezing in place when weights are scaled too high, whereas MPBRS preserves the optimal policy and achieves the task even with weights increased 500-fold.

Provided that basic joint mappings and nominal default poses are specified, walking policies for nine diverse humanoids can be trained out-of-the-box using the exact same reward structure and weights.
limitations: Convergence speed is not dramatically improved, showing limited reduction in the number of training steps compared to the baseline.
Evaluations remain confined to simulation in IsaacLab, without physical hardware validation (the sim-to-real gap remains unverified).
Tuning low-level PD controller gains for each robot and specifying baseline metadata like target base heights still rely on manual setup.
